records.content: News Sports Ticket Lifestyle Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals NEWS Florida dengue cases surge to 296, largest US outbreak in decades State adds 44 more cases C. A. Bridges Cheryl McCloud USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Oct. 9, 2026, 10:44 a.m. ET Florida has reported 296 locally acquired dengue fever cases this year, the largest outbreak in the United States in decades. The majority of cases, 259, have been confirmed in Hillsborough County, where one death has been reported. Several counties have declared states of emergency to expedite mosquito control, with 16 counties under a mosquito-borne illness alert or advisory. Florida reported 44 new locally acquired cases of dengue fever in one week, according to the latest update from the Florida Department of Health. The disease is also called breakbone fever, due to the pain it causes. That brings the statewide total to 296 for the year as of Oct. 3, the largest outbreak in the United States in decades. The previous highest number of Florida cases in recent memory was 199 in 2023. In 2025, Florida reported 62 cases for the year. Shop Amazon for mosquito repellents The bulk of the cases have been in Hillsborough County, which has 259 confirmed cases, while other locally acquired cases have been reported in seven other counties. Broward County reported its first confirmed human dengue case on Oct. 5. One death was confirmed in Hillsborough County, identified as 80-year-old Gay Small, who died of “dengue infection” along with septic shock and multi-organ failure, according to a death certificate. The previous largest outbreak was in Hawaii's Big Island, where 264 local cases were reported in the six months between September 2015 and March 2016. Florida's surge began three months ago. ➤ Prevent dengue at home in Florida with this 10-minute mosquito inspection Three Tampa Bay-area counties — Pasco, Hillsborough, and Pinellas — have declared states of emergency to expedite mosquito control operations and cut through paperwork for emergency response. Currently, 16 counties are under either a mosquito-borne illness advisory or mosquito-borne illness alert. West Nile virus and chikungunya — which are also transmitted by mosquitoes — have also been reported in Florida this year, but in far fewer numbers than dengue. Another human case of West Nile was reported in Holmes County in the period of Sept. 27 - Oct. 3, bringing the state total to seven for the year. No new chikungunya cases were reported. ➤ Dengue cases keep climbing in Florida. This is how to protect yourself There have also been 262 dengue cases associated with international travel reported in Florida this year, 215 of which were from travel from Cuba, according to the FDOH. Most of the cases were reported in Miami-Dade County. Although these cases were not locally acquired, mosquitoes that bite infected people in the state can transmit the disease to others. Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for, and how best to prevent mosquito bites, including advice from the Florida Department of Health. Dengue still surging in Florida. See counties reporting mosquito-borne illnesses According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Oct. 3, there have been 296 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported in seven counties, which is up from 252 reported Oct. 1. There have also been seven positive samples of West Nile virus and one case of chikungunya. Dengue: 296 cases 259 in Hillsborough County 20 in Pinellas County 8 in Miami-Dade County 3 in Orange County 3 in Pasco County 1 in Broward County 1 in Palm Beach County 1 in Polk County West Nile: 7 cases 2 in Alachua County 2 in Duval County (1 an asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Holmes County 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Walton County Chikungunya: 1 case 1 in Miami-Dade County What's causing the Florida outbreak of dengue fever? One reason for the surge in dengue cases is due to a comibation of "climatic and human factors that create ideal conditions" for the types of mosquitoes that spread dengue, West Nile and the chikungunya viruses, said Eva Buckner, associate professor and extension specialist with the UF/IFAS Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory via email Sept. 23. Those factors include warmer temperatures, increased rainfall and standing water, and human travel from other countries with outbreaks. Health data show that 215 of the 262 Florida cases acquired from outside the country were people who had recently traveled from Cuba. Most of the cases were DENV-2, one of the disease's four serotypes and the serotype behind Cuba's current epidemic, where fuel shortages are hampering fumigation efforts, according to Forbes. 16 mosquito-borne illness alerts, advisories issued for these Florida counties A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties: Brevard Broward Holmes Leon Manatee Martin Palm Beach Polk Walton A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Duval Hillsborough Miami-Dade Orange Pasco Pinellas "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." All Florida residents could take precautions to avoid mosquito-borne illnesses "Residents throughout the state should continue to take precautions from mosquito-borne illnesses by appropriately applying bug spray, avoiding areas with high mosquito populations, and wearing long pants and shirts when possible — especially during sunrise and sunset when mosquitos are most active," said Isabella White, FDOH press secretary via email Sept. 23. White said FDOH "continues to coordinate with local mosquito control partners to support surveillance and targeted response efforts in affected areas. These efforts help reduce mosquito populations, limit the risk of disease transmission, and protect residents across Florida." What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Why is dengue called 'breakbone fever?' Dengue is sometimes called “breakbone fever” because, in addition to fever, "it can cause severe aches and pains, especially in the legs, joints, and back," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue does not actually cause bones to break, according to YaleMedicine. Is dengue contagious? Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people through bites. The Centers for Disease Control said a woman infected with the dengue virus during pregnancy could pass the virus to her fetus, causing death to the fetus, low birth weight, or premature birth. Can dengue be treated? "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body’s immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. C.A. A new modelling study published in PLOS Medicine has now provided the most detailed picture to date of how intensely dengue virus has circulated across Mexico between 2016 and 2023, both overall and separately for each of the virus’s four serotypes. By analysing more than 833,000 probable or confirmed dengue cases reported to the country’s National Epidemiological Surveillance System, known as SINAVE, the research team quantified the force of infection, a measure of the rate at which susceptible individuals acquire infection, across 27 Mexican states. The results reveal striking spatial, temporal and serotype-specific heterogeneities that have important implications for how the country, and the wider region, plans vaccination strategies, vector control campaigns and outbreak preparedness. The study, led by Oliver S. Simmons and Ilaria Dorigatti together with colleagues at Mexican research institutions, set out to fill two important gaps in the understanding of dengue epidemiology. First, while earlier work had mapped long-term average spatial patterns of dengue risk in Mexico, nobody had systematically characterised how transmission intensity shifts from year to year across the country. Second, the relative transmissibility of the four dengue virus serotypes, DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4, remains poorly characterised both in Mexico and globally, despite the fact that these serotypes differ genetically and can dominate outbreaks at different times and places. Understanding these differences matters because infection with one serotype confers long-lasting immunity only against that serotype, while secondary infection with a different serotype is a well-established risk factor for severe disease. To address these questions, the researchers employed catalytic models, a class of mathematical models originally developed to describe age patterns of infection for vaccine-preventable diseases. These models use the age distribution of cases, combined with case counts over time, to estimate the force of infection without requiring population-wide serological surveys. Crucially, the team developed a new serotype-specific extension of these established models, allowing them to estimate how intensely each of the four serotypes was transmitting in each state and year. This methodological advance means that routinely collected case-notification data, which health ministries already gather as part of standard surveillance, can be repurposed to yield insights that would otherwise require expensive and logistically demanding seroprevalence studies. The analysis confirmed that dengue transmission in Mexico is far from uniform. Large spatial heterogeneities emerged, with some states experiencing consistently higher force of infection than others, reflecting differences in climate, urbanisation, mosquito abundance, human mobility and surveillance capacity. Equally notable were the temporal patterns: transmission intensity fluctuated considerably from year to year, underscoring that a single snapshot of average risk can be misleading for planning purposes. In years of intense transmission, a state’s population may experience a rapid accumulation of immunity, only for that same population to remain relatively untouched in subsequent years. This year-to-year volatility means that cumulative estimates of infection burden can conceal periods of both quiescence and explosive epidemic growth. The serotype-specific findings are among the most significant contributions of the study. DENV-1 and DENV-2, according to the model estimates, have historically circulated at high levels across Mexico, making them the dominant drivers of the country’s dengue burden during the study period. In contrast, DENV-4 exhibited low transmission intensity throughout the eight years analysed. Perhaps most concerning for public health planners was the evidence of increasing DENV-3 transmission intensity in several states in recent years, a trend that coincided with large outbreaks. Because many younger Mexicans may never have been exposed to DENV-3, its re-emergence creates a large susceptible population at risk of primary infection, while older cohorts previously exposed to this serotype decades ago face the possibility of secondary infection with a now-circulating different serotype, a scenario associated with elevated risk of severe dengue. The mechanistic underpinnings of these serotype-specific patterns are complex. Dengue virus transmission depends on the Aedes aegypti mosquito vector, whose abundance and susceptibility to infection can vary, as can the intrinsic fitness of each viral serotype. Differences in the force of infection between serotypes may reflect a combination of viral characteristics, such as replication efficiency in the mosquito and human host, and herd immunity dynamics, whereby a serotype that circulated widely in the past leaves fewer susceptible individuals available for future transmission. The modelling framework cannot fully disentangle these mechanisms on its own, but by generating comparable, state-level estimates of serotype-specific transmission intensity, it provides the empirical foundation upon which such mechanistic questions can be addressed in future work. The study also highlights the crucial role of diagnostics in making serotype-specific inference possible. Extensive reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction, or RT-PCR, testing during the study period allowed many cases to be attributed to a specific infecting serotype, and the authors emphasise that newly available rapid diagnostic tests capable of discerning the infecting serotype could further improve this picture. As these tests become more widely deployed, surveillance systems in Mexico and elsewhere will be better positioned to track which serotypes are circulating in near real time, information that is directly relevant to decisions about when and where to deploy interventions. The timing is particularly significant given that Mexico has introduced dengue vaccination programmes, and vaccine effectiveness and deployment strategy can depend on the local transmission intensity and the serotype composition of circulating viruses. The authors are careful to note an important limitation: the serotype-specific estimates may be affected by heterogeneities in how cases are reported across states and over time. Surveillance intensity, health-seeking behaviour, access to healthcare and diagnostic practices all vary geographically and can shift between years, and disentangling genuine changes in transmission from artefacts of the reporting system remains a task for future validation studies. Nevertheless, the scale of the dataset, spanning 833,629 cases across 27 states and eight years, lends considerable weight to the broad patterns identified, and the consistency of the findings with known epidemiological events, such as the DENV-3 resurgence coinciding with large outbreaks, supports their plausibility. The wider context makes this work especially timely. Mexico and the Americas region as a whole have experienced rising dengue incidence in recent years, and there are widespread concerns that changing climatic conditions, including warmer temperatures and shifting rainfall patterns, may expand the geographic range and seasonal window of Aedes mosquito activity, thereby enhancing transmission in the future. In this environment, accurate estimates of who remains susceptible to which serotype, and where and when transmission is most intense, become essential inputs for targeting vaccination, vector control and clinical preparedness. The methods developed in this study contribute to a better understanding of the past and current burden of dengue infection and can help refine assessments of the potential impact of existing and new interventions, from next-generation vaccines to Wolbachia-based biocontrol strategies. Ultimately, the study demonstrates the power of mining routinely collected surveillance data with appropriately sophisticated models. Rather than relying solely on costly serological surveys, public health authorities can extract detailed, serotype-resolved pictures of transmission intensity from the case notifications they already gather, provided that diagnostic testing is sufficiently extensive and that reporting heterogeneities are acknowledged and, where possible, corrected for. As dengue continues to expand its footprint across the Americas under the combined pressures of urbanisation, connectivity and climate change, approaches of this kind offer a practical route toward the granular, timely evidence base that controlling this evolving threat will demand. records.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Medical Dengue fever cases are on the rise in Hanoi, raising concerns about a potential outbreak. Experts warn that dengue fever patients can develop severe symptoms within just a few days, especially if they are complacent after the fever subsides or self-medicate without a doctor's prescription. Báo Đầu tư•14/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 According to the Hanoi Center for Disease Control (CDC), from October 2nd to the present, the city has recorded 400 cases of dengue fever in 81 wards and communes. This week, the city recorded 12 new outbreaks, bringing the cumulative total from the beginning of the year to 4,351 cases in 120 wards and communes with 193 outbreaks. Currently, 27 outbreaks remain active. Although the number of cases since the beginning of the year is lower than the average for the 2021-2025 period, data from this week shows that the disease is still circulating in the city. Notably, the period from September to November each year is when Hanoi intensifies surveillance and implements dengue fever prevention and control measures. Currently, dengue fever vaccines are available in Vietnam, adding another preventive measure alongside mosquito control. Many dengue fever patients are hospitalized with thrombocytopenia, bleeding, and liver damage. Doctors warn that from the 3rd to the 7th day of the illness, even if the fever has subsided, patients are still at risk of developing severe symptoms, including dengue shock, if not monitored and treated promptly. Recently, the number of dengue fever cases in Gia Lam commune and surrounding areas has been on the rise. At the Infectious Diseases Department of Gia Lam General Hospital, many patients are admitted with symptoms such as thrombocytopenia, hemoconcentration, bleeding, and other disorders requiring close monitoring. Some cases have developed serious complications such as gastrointestinal bleeding, hypotension, elevated liver enzymes, and liver damage. According to Dr. Ngo Trong Hieu, Head of the Infectious Diseases Department at Gia Lam General Hospital, what is worrying is that many people still consider dengue fever to be just a common fever. In the early days, when symptoms such as fever, fatigue, and body aches appear, many people self-medicate at home, believing it to be just the flu or a fever due to a change in weather. Only when abdominal pain, vomiting, extreme fatigue, or unusual bleeding occurs do patients seek medical attention. Meanwhile, dengue fever can progress very rapidly. Some patients may be alert and able to eat in the early days, but then suddenly show warning signs of worsening condition, requiring close monitoring and intensive treatment. Notably, the period from the 3rd to the 7th day after the onset of fever is usually the time when patients need to be especially vigilant. This is the period when increased vascular permeability, plasma leakage, blood concentration, thrombocytopenia, and other dangerous complications may occur. According to Dr. Ngo Trong Hieu, one common mistake is that patients assume they have recovered and stop monitoring their condition because their body temperature has decreased and their fever has subsided. In reality, the fever-reducing phase may coincide with the onset of warning signs of severe dengue fever. Symptoms that require special attention include severe or progressively worsening abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, extreme fatigue, lethargy, restlessness, bleeding gums, nosebleeds, vomiting blood, black stools, or unusual vaginal bleeding. Decreased urination, cold hands and feet, and cold, clammy skin may also indicate circulatory disorders and a risk of shock. Doctors advise that patients should not wait until all symptoms appear before going to the hospital. As soon as there are warning signs or unusual changes in health, patients should seek immediate medical attention to assess the severity of the illness and receive timely intervention. At the Infectious Diseases Department of Gia Lam General Hospital, doctors treated patient D.D.A., who had dengue fever with thrombocytopenia (low platelet count). The patient was admitted for monitoring, underwent necessary tests, and was prescribed platelet transfusions based on clinical assessment. After the infusion, the patient continued to be monitored for signs of bleeding and laboratory test results. Throughout the treatment process, the patient's health condition improved. Based on this case, Dr. Ngo Trong Hieu noted that thrombocytopenia is a common symptom in dengue fever patients, but not every case of thrombocytopenia requires platelet transfusion. The decision to transfuse must be based on the clinical condition, the degree of thrombocytopenia, bleeding manifestations, and related risk factors. Platelet transfusions are not routinely performed solely to increase platelet count. Patients should adhere to their doctor's assessment and instructions, and avoid attempting to increase platelet count using unproven methods. For dengue fever cases where doctors recommend home monitoring, patients need rest, adequate hydration, and may use oral rehydration solutions as directed. They should also closely monitor their health. Family members should assist in observing the patient's alertness, fluid intake, frequency of urination, abdominal pain, vomiting, and any signs of unusual bleeding. You may also like In symptomatic treatment, patients can use paracetamol to reduce fever as directed by healthcare professionals. Absolutely do not self-administer aspirin or ibuprofen due to the risk of increased bleeding. Self-administering intravenous fluids at home also carries many risks if not properly assessed and prescribed. Doctors emphasize that not all dengue fever cases require hospitalization. However, the decision to monitor at home must be based on professional assessment, and patients need clear instructions on when to return for follow-up appointments and what signs require immediate hospitalization. Besides early detection and timely treatment, prevention remains crucial in the context of a rising number of cases. According to Dr. Ngo Trong Hieu, the core measure is controlling disease-carrying mosquitoes, eliminating breeding grounds for larvae and pupae, and reducing the risk of mosquito bites. Residents should regularly inspect their living areas, collecting bottles, plastic containers, old tires, and other items that can collect water. Household water containers must be tightly covered and cleaned regularly. Additionally, each family should maintain the habit of sleeping under mosquito nets, even during the day, wearing long-sleeved clothing, and using appropriate mosquito control measures. In particular, families with a member infected with dengue fever need to take extra precautions against mosquito bites to protect the patient and reduce the risk of mosquitoes sucking blood from infected individuals and then transmitting the disease to others. Currently, dengue fever vaccines are available in Vietnam, adding another preventive measure alongside mosquito control. People can visit vaccination centers for advice on age, eligibility, and appropriate vaccination schedules. Experts advise that dengue fever can be effectively monitored and treated if detected early, the severity of the disease is accurately assessed, and professional guidelines are followed. However, people should not be complacent about changes in their bodies, especially during the period from the 3rd to the 7th day. The disappearance of fever does not mean the dangerous phase is over. Proactively seeking medical attention, closely monitoring warning signs, and promptly going to a healthcare facility are crucial factors in minimizing the risk of shock, severe bleeding, and life-threatening complications. In addition, many people make mistakes in using medication during dengue fever treatment. Associate Professor, Doctor of Pharmacy Nguyen Tuan Dung, senior professional advisor of Long Chau Pharmacy and Vaccination System, said that paracetamol (acetaminophen) is used to reduce fever in dengue fever cases. Meanwhile, patients should not self-medicate with aspirin, ibuprofen, or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as diclofenac or naproxen. It's worth noting that these are all fairly common medications, often thought of by people when experiencing fever, headache, or body aches. Dengue fever can cause thrombocytopenia and blood clotting disorders. In this context, the effects of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) on platelet function may increase the risk of bleeding. Aspirin causes irreversible inhibition of platelet aggregation, while other NSAIDs can also reduce platelet aggregation to varying degrees. This group of drugs can also damage the gastric and duodenal mucosa, thereby increasing the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding. Another risk relates to kidney function. People with dengue fever may experience reduced circulating volume due to plasma leakage. NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin synthesis in the kidneys, which can decrease renal blood flow and increase the risk of acute kidney injury. Furthermore, the strong pain-relieving effects of the medication may partially mask symptoms, making it more difficult to recognize warning signs of worsening illness. For adults weighing over 50 kg, paracetamol is typically administered at a dose of 500-1000 mg per dose, every 4-6 hours as needed, with a total dose not exceeding 4000 mg in 24 hours. However, the total amount of paracetamol must be calculated from all medications the patient is currently taking. Individuals with liver disease, kidney disease, frequent alcohol use, or malnutrition (weighing less than 50 kg) should exercise particular caution. Dosage and dosing intervals may need adjustment depending on individual circumstances and should be guided by a healthcare professional. You may also like A common situation is that patients have taken ibuprofen or aspirin before knowing they have or suspect they have dengue fever. Associate Professor, Doctor of Pharmacy Nguyen Tuan Dung advises patients not to panic and to absolutely not to self-medicate to "counteract" the medication they have taken. The necessary action is to stop taking aspirin, ibuprofen, and other NSAIDs, then inform the doctor specifically about the name of the medication, dosage, time of use, and number of doses taken so that an appropriate assessment can be made. If fever reduction or pain relief is needed, patients can use paracetamol at an appropriate dose. More importantly, their health condition should continue to be closely monitored to promptly detect any abnormal signs. Another risk comes from combination cold and flu medications. Many products already contain paracetamol, but users don't pay attention to the ingredient and then take additional paracetamol separately to reduce fever. Combining the doses from multiple products can lead to an overdose. Some cold and flu medications may contain ibuprofen, aspirin, or other ingredients unsuitable for people suspected of having dengue fever. Therefore, experts advise against self-medicating with combination cold and flu medications during this period. Besides using the correct medication, one development in dengue fever that patients often overlook is the reduction or disappearance of fever. Associate Professor, Doctor of Pharmacy Nguyen Tuan Dung notes that the disappearance of fever does not mean recovery. When body temperature returns to normal, patients can stop taking fever-reducing medication but must continue to monitor their health. The critical phase of the illness can occur around the 3rd to 8th day after infection, especially around the time the patient's fever subsides. Several serious complications can develop during this period and progress within 24-48 hours. Patients should seek immediate medical attention if they experience any unusual symptoms such as severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums or nosebleeds, vomiting blood, black or bloody stools, rapid breathing, lethargy, restlessness, cold hands and feet, or decreased urination. Some children carry the virus with barely a symptom, while others with the same infection progress to hospitalization with severe plasma leakage and shock. A new study of Cambodian children infected with dengue virus suggests that part of the answer lies not in how much antibody the immune system produces, but in the quality and specificity of the antibody-secreting cells mobilized during the acute phase of infection. The research, published in PLOS Pathogens, was led by Amandine Trouchet and colleagues working across institutes in France and Cambodia, including teams at the Institut Pasteur and the Institut Pasteur du Cambodge. The investigators set out to examine a question that has long frustrated dengue immunologists: which antibody features actually mediate protection in humans? Although dengue vaccines and monoclonal antibody therapies have been developed, the correlates of protection against severe disease remain poorly defined, in large part because the human antibody response to dengue is exceptionally complex. That complexity stems from the structure of the virus itself. Dengue virus is coated with 180 copies of the envelope protein, known simply as E, which is the principal target of neutralizing antibodies. On the mature virion surface, E proteins are arranged as 90 homodimers, and this dimeric arrangement creates quaternary epitopes—antigenic surfaces that exist only when two E proteins are paired together. Antibodies that recognize these quaternary epitopes tend to be highly neutralizing and broadly reactive across the four dengue virus serotypes, whereas antibodies that bind only to isolated E monomers are frequently weakly neutralizing or even non-neutralizing, and in some contexts can contribute to antibody-dependent enhancement, the phenomenon in which pre-existing antibodies facilitate infection of cells by a different serotype. To dissect the antibody response at the level of individual cells, the team turned to droplet-based microfluidics, a technology that allows thousands of single antibody-secreting cells to be captured and analyzed in parallel. Each cell is enclosed in its own microscopic droplet together with fluorescently labeled viral antigens, so that the antibodies secreted by that single cell can be imaged as they bind to the antigen in real time. Using this approach, the researchers profiled more than 3,300 individual IgG-secreting cells from pediatric patients enrolled in a Cambodian cohort, comparing children with subclinical dengue infections against those who were hospitalized with symptomatic disease. The cohort was carefully structured to allow meaningful comparisons. The children had experienced either acute DENV1 or DENV2 infection, and the analysis focused on post-primary infections, meaning the patients were responding to dengue for at least the second time. This distinction matters because primary and secondary dengue infections generate qualitatively different antibody repertoires, and secondary infections carry a substantially higher risk of severe outcomes, a pattern thought to be driven in part by cross-reactive but poorly neutralizing antibodies generated during the first encounter with the virus. The first major finding was quantitative. Hospitalized patients had significantly fewer IgG-secreting cells in their circulation than children with subclinical infections, despite the fact that the cells they did possess secreted IgG at comparable rates. Moreover, when the researchers calculated the frequency of dengue E-specific antibody-secreting cells as a proportion of the total IgG-secreting population, they found no significant difference between the two groups. In other words, the immune systems of hospitalized children were not failing to target dengue specifically; they were simply mounting a smaller overall antibody-secreting response, leaving fewer antigen-specific cells available to fight the infection. The second finding concerned antibody affinity, a measure of how tightly an antibody binds its target. When the secreted antibodies from single cells were tested against the DENV1 envelope dimer, the antibodies from hospitalized patients showed a threefold lower average affinity than those from subclinical cases. Affinity matters enormously in antiviral defense: high-affinity antibodies neutralize virus more efficiently, persist longer in memory, and are more likely to mediate protective Fc-dependent functions. A threefold reduction across a population of antibody-secreting cells suggests that the germinal center reaction—the specialized structure in lymphoid tissue where B cells refine their antibodies through mutation and selection—was less effective in the children who went on to develop severe disease. The most striking qualitative difference emerged when the researchers probed the specificity of the antibodies for quaternary epitopes. Because quaternary epitopes depend on the dimeric arrangement of E on the virion, antibodies that bind the E dimer but not the E monomer are considered quaternary-epitope-specific. When the team compared binding to dimeric versus monomeric E protein, they found that antibodies recognizing quaternary epitopes were detected exclusively in the subclinical group. Hospitalized patients, by contrast, predominantly produced monomer-reactive antibodies—antibodies that bind the envelope protein in isolation and therefore, by inference, are less likely to recognize the authentic viral surface with the precision required for potent neutralization. Taken together, these results sketch a coherent picture of what distinguishes a protective dengue antibody response from a failing one. Children who weathered infection without hospitalization generated larger numbers of antibody-secreting cells, with higher average affinity for the envelope dimer and a clear representation of quaternary-epitope-specific clones. Hospitalized children produced fewer cells, of lower affinity, skewed toward monomer reactivity. The authors propose that dengue severity may be linked to the inefficient generation of sufficient numbers of high-affinity, broadly reactive antigen-specific IgG-secreting cells during post-primary infection, rather than to any single deficit in antibody quantity alone. The study carries implications for vaccine design and for the long-standing effort to define immune correlates of protection against dengue. Vaccines that reliably elicit quaternary-epitope-specific, high-affinity antibodies—rather than merely high titers of cross-reactive monomer-binding antibodies—may better recapitulate the response pattern associated with subclinical outcomes. The single-cell microfluidic approach also offers a template for future studies, since it captures the true diversity of the antibody-secreting cell population rather than averaging signals across bulk serum. As the authors note, the antibody features that mediate protection in humans remain poorly defined, and this work in a well-characterized Cambodian pediatric cohort provides some of the clearest evidence yet that the monoclonal composition of the early antibody response, not just its magnitude, shapes the clinical trajectory of dengue virus infection. Home Business Lifestyle Tutorials Technology Politics Education Sports Public Info Automotive Opinion Economy Health Temukan lebih banyak Berita Politik Cari Referensi Berita Gaya Hidup Home Health Hawaii Confirms Ninth Travel Related Dengue Case in 2026 Hawaii Confirms Ninth Travel Related Dengue Case in 2026 Ashley Morgan Published Oct 15, 2026 - 01:30 2 Reads Last Update Oct 15, 2026 - 01:30 Share WhatsApp Joe Raedle | Getty Images Smallest Font Largest Font Hawaii health officials have confirmed a ninth dengue case in the state in 2026 after a traveler became infected while visiting a region where the virus is common. Announced on October 13 and 14, the case was identified on Oahu, prompting inspections and mosquito control measures as authorities work to limit local transmission following recent heavy rainfall. The Hawaii Department of Health said the new infection has no known connection to previously reported cases. All nine dengue cases recorded in Hawaii this year involved travel to Pacific Island countries and territories, and officials said the disease has not become established in the state. Health department teams have been dispatched to the affected area to identify mosquito breeding sites and implement control measures. Although mosquitoes capable of transmitting dengue live in Hawaii, officials consider the current risk of local transmission low. The department is urging residents to remove standing water from outdoor containers, including buckets, planters, rain barrels, cups and water-catching plants. Recent rainfall can create additional breeding sites, allowing mosquito populations to grow around homes and workplaces. Dengue spreads when a mosquito bites an infected person and subsequently transmits the virus by biting another person. Symptoms can include fever, nausea, vomiting, rash and body aches, generally lasting two to seven days. Most patients recover within a week, although severe illness is possible. The department recommends that travelers visiting affected regions use an Environmental Protection Agency-registered insect repellent, wear long-sleeved shirts and long pants, and sleep in air-conditioned or screened rooms or under insecticide-treated bed nets. Travelers returning from areas where dengue occurs should continue preventing mosquito bites for three weeks. According to the department's guidance, people who develop symptoms within two weeks of returning from an affected area should seek medical evaluation. Healthcare providers and individuals who suspect dengue infection can contact the Hawaii Department of Health's Disease Reporting Line at 808-586-4586. Florida is facing a separate and more extensive outbreak of locally acquired dengue infections. A Florida surveillance report covering cases through October 3 recorded 296 locally acquired cases statewide, including 259 in Hillsborough County, according to MedicalDaily. The county had increased aerial and ground mosquito treatments as officials assessed whether to extend its local emergency declaration, which was scheduled to expire October 15. Hillsborough County's mosquito control operations include daytime helicopter applications of Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis, or Bti, to standing water to target mosquito larvae. An October 11 report from Osprey Observer said treatments were planned from October 12 through October 16 in Bloomingdale, Palm River, East Tampa and East Lake, where mosquito surveillance had indicated dengue virus activity. Florida Department of Health officials in Hillsborough County have emphasized that mosquito treatments alone cannot eliminate the risk. Removing water-holding containers remains an important part of prevention because mosquitoes that transmit dengue can breed in small amounts of standing water. Public health leaders in Karnataka, India, have also called for continuous dengue prevention rather than relying primarily on seasonal outbreak responses. A multi-stakeholder meeting in Bengaluru brought together government representatives, researchers, public health institutions and civil society organizations to develop a four-point action plan. Karnataka Health and Family Welfare Minister U.T. Khader Fareed said the recent decline in cases should not lead to complacency. He called for stronger surveillance, diagnostics, mosquito monitoring, vaccination research and community-based prevention as environmental conditions continue to influence transmission. School Education and Literacy Minister Madhu Bangarappa highlighted the role of schools in public awareness and prevention. Participants proposed year-round education, stronger links between community screening and healthcare, coordinated state and municipal surveillance data, and investment in locally adapted technology for mosquito monitoring. That brings the total number of cases in Orange County this year to 5. Orange County Mosquito Control plans to spray for mosquitos in Apopka and Pine Hills over the next two weeks. ORANGE COUNTY, Fla. - Two more cases of locally-acquired dengue fever have been reported in Orange County, according to the Florida Department of Health, bringing the total number of cases this year to five. Orange County officials plan to conduct more sprays targeting mosquitos known to transmit dengue fever. Dengue fever cases in Orange County. Here's where. By the numbers: According to the Florida Department of Health and Orange County Mosquito Control, the five cases have been reported in Pine Hills and Apopka: Sept. 1: 1 confirmed case in Pine Hills area Sept. 18: 2 confirmed cases in the Apopka area Oct. 12: 2 more confirmed cases in the Apopka area What we don't know: Officials have not released specifics about the persons who've contracted the virus, nor updates on their conditions. What is dengue fever? Why you should care: Dengue is a virus spread through bites from two species of mosquitoes, Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, according to Florida health officials. Both are found in Florida. When someone is infected, it can lead to dengue fever, a sometimes painful, debilitating disease. While rare, if symptoms are left untreated, it can be deadly. Signs and symptoms Symptoms typically appear 3-14 days after being bitten by an infected mosquito, and usually last 4-7 days, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Florida Department of Health: Sudden fever Severe headache Eye pain Muscle and joint pain Bleeding Vomiting and diarrhea There is no treatment for dengue fever. However, the CDC recommends people treat their symptoms early to manage potential complications. Orange County to spray for mosquitoes Timeline: Orange County Mosquito Control said it plans to conduct aerial spraying in Apopka and Pine Hills over the next several weeks to target mosquito populations known to transmit Dengue Fever. When will those sprays happen? Officials said residents will be notified at least 48 hours in advance via the county's social media channels, website, and through OC Alert notification. Click here to sign up to receive an alert. Tips to avoid mosquito bites What you can do: "It is very important for residents to ensure that there is no standing water on their property. We encourage residents to walk around their yards after a storm and drain any standing water, toss out anything that could hold water, and protect yourself with long sleeves, pants, and EPA-approved mosquito repellent," said Steve Harrison, manager of Orange County Mosquito Control in a statement. Health officials are urging residents to take steps to prevent mosquito bites: Use insect repellent on exposed skin or clothing Remove standing water to stop mosquitoes from breeding Keep doors, exterior windows closed More on dengue fever Dig deeper: CDC: Dengue fever FDOH: Dengue fever in Florida Florida weekly arbovirus surveillance report Orange County Mosquito Control The Source: This story uses information gathered from the Florida Department of Health in Orange County (FDOH), Orange County Mosquito Control, the Florida Department of Health's Arbovirus Surveillance report, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and previous reporting by FOX 35. records.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Medical Hanoi records 400 dengue fever cases in one week: Warning signs that cannot be ignored. GĐXH - Experts warn that dengue fever patients can experience severe symptoms within just a few days, especially if they are complacent after the fever subsides or self-medicate without a doctor's prescription. Báo Gia đình và Xã hội•13/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Dengue fever is on the rise, and many people easily mistake it for a common fever. According to the Hanoi Center for Disease Control (CDC), from October 2nd to October 9th, 2026, the city recorded 400 cases of dengue fever across 81 wards and communes. During the week, the city recorded 12 new outbreaks. Cumulatively from the beginning of the year to date, Hanoi has had 4,351 cases in 120 wards and communes with 193 outbreaks. Currently, 27 outbreaks remain active. Dengue fever is on the rise, and many people easily mistake it for a common fever. (Illustrative image.) Although the number of cases since the beginning of the year is lower than the average for the 2021-2025 period, data from this week shows that the disease is still circulating in the city. Notably, the period from September to November each year is when Hanoi intensifies surveillance and implements dengue fever prevention and control measures. Khám phá thêm Tìm hiểu lịch sử Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch Khám phá ĐNA According to experts, dengue fever is an infectious disease caused by the dengue virus, transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. Initial symptoms usually include a sudden high fever, headache, eye pain, muscle and joint aches, possibly accompanied by nausea or a rash. These symptoms are easily mistaken for other viral fevers, leading patients to self-medicate or delay seeking medical attention. In fact, over the past period, many hospitals in Hanoi have received and treated numerous cases of dengue fever with complicated symptoms. In September 2026 alone, the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases reported that it had received and treated dengue fever cases with diverse manifestations, including many severe cases. Notably, a 37-year-old female patient initially thought she only had a common cold and self-medicated with fever-reducing drugs, but to no avail. On the second day of her illness, she developed severe headaches, high fever, and bleeding gums, and was subsequently diagnosed with Dengue fever. According to Dr. Nguyen Thanh Binh, Deputy Head of the Virology - Parasitology Department at the Central Hospital for Tropical Diseases, people often make several mistakes when contracting dengue fever, leading to delays in detection and monitoring. One common mistake is self-medicating when fever and headache first appear. In particular, before ruling out dengue fever, patients should not self-medicate with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), as these drugs can increase the risk of bleeding. Lowering the fever does not mean the danger is over. You may also like According to Dr. Binh, from the 3rd to the 7th day of dengue fever, especially when the patient's fever begins to subside or disappear, some cases may enter a dangerous phase. At this time, increased vascular permeability can lead to plasma leakage; in severe cases, it can cause decreased circulating volume, hypotension, and shock. Platelets may also decrease, and the patient may exhibit hemorrhagic symptoms. Doctors advise people not to be complacent when contracting dengue fever. Photo: National Hospital for Tropical Diseases. Meanwhile, when body temperature returns to near normal, many people become complacent, assuming the illness is cured and neglecting monitoring. In reality, this is a stage that requires close monitoring to promptly detect any warning signs. Therefore, if diagnosed with dengue fever and being monitored at home, patients need to adhere to their scheduled follow-up appointments, monitor for any unusual symptoms, and follow the instructions of healthcare professionals. Do not discontinue monitoring simply because your body temperature has returned to normal. The elderly , young children, pregnant women, and people with underlying conditions such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, kidney disease, or those undergoing cancer treatment require special attention. If dengue fever symptoms are suspected, these individuals should seek medical attention early so that a doctor can assess the risk and provide appropriate monitoring guidance. For fever-reducing medication, patients should only use it as directed by a healthcare professional. Do not self-medicate with aspirin, ibuprofen, or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) as this may increase the risk of bleeding. Do not self-medicate with antibiotics, herbal remedies, or products of unknown ingredients. Currently, there is no specific, routinely used treatment for dengue fever to eliminate the dengue virus. Care and treatment mainly focus on close monitoring, symptom management, and timely intervention in case of complications. Patients should not self-administer intravenous fluids at home, as inappropriate fluid replacement can be dangerous. In particular, when symptoms such as persistent high fever, severe abdominal pain (especially in the liver and epigastric region), frequent vomiting, nosebleeds, bleeding gums, vomiting blood, black stools, irregular menstruation, extreme fatigue, lethargy, cold hands and feet, shortness of breath, or any other unusual symptoms appear, patients should immediately go to a medical facility for timely assessment and treatment to avoid possible complications. Actively eliminate mosquitoes and destroy breeding grounds for Aedes mosquitoes. You may also like According to experts, alongside early detection of disease symptoms, preventing mosquito bites and eliminating breeding grounds for Aedes mosquitoes are crucial measures to limit the transmission of dengue fever. People should cover water containers tightly, regularly clean jars, pots, buckets, and basins; change the water in flower vases, remove stagnant water from trays, old tires, and other items around the house. They should sleep under mosquito nets, wear long-sleeved clothing, use appropriate mosquito repellents, and cooperate with local authorities in environmental sanitation, mosquito larva eradication, and chemical spraying when instructed. In addition, people can proactively learn about and get vaccinated against dengue fever according to appropriate guidelines and indications. With dengue fever cases still being recorded in many wards and communes in Hanoi, experts advise that each family should proactively take preventive measures and not be complacent when symptoms such as fever appear. Early recognition of warning signs, timely medical examination, and adherence to treatment guidelines are crucial factors in limiting the risk of severe complications from dengue fever. Article will play after ad... Playing in :00 A A A Kaua‘i mosquito trapping (Aug. 25, 2022). PC: Hawaiʻi Department of Land and Natural Resources The Hawai‘i Department of Health reports identifying a new travel-related dengue virus case on Oʻahu, bringing the total number of dengue cases in the state to eight for 2026. All of the cases have involved travel to Pacific Island countries and territories. The affected individual was exposed to the virus while traveling in a region where dengue is common. No connection to any prior cases in Hawaiʻi have been found. Health department teams have been deployed to conduct inspections and implement mosquito control measures in the affected area. Dengue virus is transmitted from an infected person to a mosquito and then to another person. Due to the circumstances of this case, the expected risk of transmission is low. However, with recent heavy rain, this case is a reminder for the public to eliminate standing water as much as possible. Reducing standing water helps prevent mosquito breeding and can reduce the risk of local transmission of vector-borne diseases. More information about mosquito control is available on the Vector Control Branch website. Dengue is a year-round risk in tropical and subtropical areas of Central and South America, including Brazil and Mexico; Asia, including the Philippines; the Middle East; Africa; and several Pacific islands, including American Samoa, the Federated States of Micronesia, the Republic of the Marshall Islands and the Republic of Palau. Many popular tourist destinations in the Caribbean, including Puerto Rico, are also affected. Some countries are reporting higher-than-usual numbers of dengue cases, including Bangladesh, Bolivia, Cambodia, Costa Rica, Cuba, Ecuador, Kenya, Malaysia, Maldives, Marshall Islands, Panama, Sri Lanka, Vanuatu and Vietnam. Travelers should review current, country-specific travel information for guidance on dengue risk and prevention measures at least four to six weeks before traveling. For current travel health information and guidance, visit the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) travel website. Anyone planning to travel to or who has recently visited an area with dengue risk may be at risk for infection. The CDC advises travelers to take standard precautions when visiting such areas. These include using an Environmental Protection Agency-registered insect repellent, wearing long-sleeved shirts and long pants outdoors, as well as sleeping in air-conditioned rooms, rooms with window screens or under insecticide-treated bed nets. Travelers returning from areas with dengue risk should take precautions to prevent mosquito bites for three weeks. If dengue symptoms develop within two weeks of returning, travelers should seek medical evaluation. Symptoms of dengue can range from mild to severe and include fever, nausea, vomiting, rash and body aches. Symptoms typically last two to seven days. While severe illness can occur, most people recover within a week. Individuals who have recently traveled and are experiencing these symptoms should contact their healthcare provider. Healthcare providers and individuals who suspect dengue infection are advised to call the Disease Reporting Line at 808-586-4586. In areas with suspected or confirmed dengue cases, Health Department vector control personnel conduct inspections and mosquito-reduction activities. Reducing mosquito populations lowers the risk of dengue transmission to others. In areas without reported dengue cases, eliminating mosquito breeding sites around the home is an important preventive measure. Mosquitoes need only small amounts of standing water to breed. Common breeding sites include buckets, water-catching plants such as bromeliads, small containers, planters, rain barrels and even cups left outside. Prevent standing water from collecting around homes and workplaces by emptying containers and other items where mosquitoes can lay eggs. records.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Medical Dengue fever and hand, foot, and mouth disease are on the rise, raising concerns about life-threatening complications. In just one week, Ho Chi Minh City recorded more than 3,100 cases of dengue fever and hand, foot, and mouth disease, with the number of hand, foot, and mouth disease cases increasing by nearly 48%. Báo Đầu tư•09/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 The infectious disease situation in Ho Chi Minh City continues to be complex, especially with dengue fever and hand, foot, and mouth disease, two diseases that can spread rapidly and cause dangerous complications if not detected and treated promptly. Worryingly, the number of hand, foot, and mouth disease cases is increasing sharply, while dengue fever remains at a high level, increasing pressure on disease prevention and control efforts. According to data from the Ho Chi Minh City Center for Disease Control (HCDC), in week 40, from September 28 to October 4, 2026, the city recorded 1,505 cases of dengue fever, a decrease of 2.3% compared to the average of the previous four weeks. Despite the slight downward trend, the number of cases remains concerning, bringing the total number of dengue fever cases from the beginning of the year to the end of week 40 to 37,369. Health experts emphasize that proactive disease prevention is of particular importance, and vaccination is one of the effective solutions for infectious diseases for which vaccines are available. Localities with high dengue fever incidence rates per 100,000 people include Con Dao Special Zone, Ngai Giao, and Minh Thanh. These areas require continued strengthening of epidemiological surveillance, control of disease-carrying mosquitoes, and handling of outbreaks to limit the risk of community spread. Meanwhile, hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) has seen an alarming increase. In week 40 alone, the city recorded 1,673 cases, a 47.8% increase compared to the average of the previous four weeks. Cumulatively from the beginning of the year to the end of week 40, Ho Chi Minh City has recorded 38,463 cases of HFMD. Areas with high incidence rates include Con Dao Special Economic Zone, Binh Khanh, and Hiep Phuoc. Thus, in just one week, these two infectious diseases have infected 3,178 people. These figures show that the risk of an epidemic still exists, especially in the context of unpredictable weather and the group learning and living activities of young children, which create conditions for disease-causing agents to spread. The worrying aspect lies not only in the number of cases but also in the risk of severe complications, even death, associated with both diseases. Dengue fever can progress rapidly from initial symptoms such as high fever, headache, and body aches to plasma leakage, shock, severe bleeding, and multi-organ failure. In particular, the dangerous phase of dengue fever usually occurs from the 3rd to the 7th day of the illness, when the patient's fever may subside or disappear. The misconception that the absence of fever means recovery can cause patients to miss warning signs, increasing the risk of serious complications. For hand, foot, and mouth disease, most cases resolve spontaneously, but some cases, especially in young children, can progress to severe complications such as neurological, cardiovascular, and respiratory problems. Symptoms such as persistently high fever, startled reactions, tremors, unsteady gait, abnormal breathing, or lethargy are warning signs that require urgent medical attention and treatment. You may also like In fact, the danger of hand, foot, and mouth disease also lies in its rapid progression, with some cases becoming severe in a short time. Children with the disease who are not closely monitored may develop life-threatening complications, especially in cases involving highly virulent enterovirus strains such as EV71. Given this situation, health experts emphasize that proactive disease prevention is of paramount importance, and vaccination is one of the effective solutions for infectious diseases for which vaccines are available. For dengue fever, Vietnam uses the Qdenga vaccine. This vaccine is administered to children aged 4 years and older and adults, including those who have previously had the disease, and helps prevent all four types of dengue virus. The vaccination schedule consists of two doses, administered three months apart. The protective efficacy is over 80%, reducing the risk of hospitalization due to dengue fever by over 90% when the full vaccination regimen is completed. Experts believe the greatest significance of the vaccine lies not only in reducing the risk of contracting the disease but also in limiting severe cases, easing the burden on the healthcare system during outbreaks, and contributing to the protection of high-risk groups such as children. However, the vaccine is not suitable for people who are hypersensitive to any of its components, pregnant women, or breastfeeding mothers. For immunocompromised individuals or those with HIV, please consult a healthcare professional for guidance tailored to your specific situation. Regarding hand, foot, and mouth disease, a notable point is that the Ministry of Health has approved a vaccine against hand, foot, and mouth disease caused by the EV71 virus, opening up opportunities to prevent severe complications of the disease. Mr. Chau Thanh Tu, Chief Pharmacist of the Pharmaceutical Professional Council at Long Chau Pharmacy and Vaccination Center, said that the unit is preparing the necessary steps to bring the vaccine to serve the Vietnamese people as soon as possible. According to Mr. Tu, vaccination is one of the important preventive measures against infectious diseases for which vaccines are available. During the period when children return to school, in addition to the risk of hand, foot, and mouth disease, parents also need to proactively prevent easily transmissible diseases such as meningococcal disease, measles, influenza, chickenpox, and whooping cough, ensuring their children receive all vaccinations on schedule after consulting with a specialist. Until hand, foot, and mouth disease vaccines are widely available, personal hygiene, environmental disinfection, infection control, and early recognition of signs of worsening symptoms remain the most important measures. You may also like With high infection rates and young children returning to in-person learning environments, coordination between families, schools, and the health sector will be crucial in breaking the chain of transmission and limiting the number of severe cases. For families with young children, early recognition of abnormal signs is crucial in limiting complications. Parents need to closely monitor the disease's progression, avoid self-medication, and take their children to a medical facility immediately if warning signs appear. Children with hand, foot, and mouth disease should stay home from school, limit contact with other children, and follow infection prevention measures as instructed by health authorities. The health sector also advises schools and preschools to strengthen hygiene in classrooms, toys, and living equipment, and proactively identify children showing symptoms of suspected illness. Close cooperation between families, schools, and health facilities will help limit the risk of outbreaks in the school environment. records.content_title: Orange County Mosquito Control plans aerial spraying to fight dengue fever outbreak
records.content: ORANGE COUNTY, Fla. — Orange County Mosquito Control officials are preparing to take to the air to fight the spread of dengue fever, as more locally acquired cases are discovered in Apopka. The latest cases bring the total number of locally acquired infections in Central Florida to five. Health officials are also investigating two additional suspected cases as concerns grow about the mosquito-borne illness. Orange County Mosquito Control Manager Steve Harrison is asking county commissioners for $150,000 to fund aerial spraying aimed at reducing the mosquito population and stopping the spread. According to the Florida Department of Health , two new locally acquired cases were identified in Apopka. “That there are two additional locally acquired cases of dengue, that brought us from the three known to now, the two additional, which gives us five. There are also two suspect cases that are being tested,” Harrison said. Harrison went before county commissioners Tuesday to request funding for the aerial spraying operation. When approved, the effort is expected to launch from Bartow on Friday, using a plane similar to the aircraft shown by mosquito control officials. The spraying would target three areas in Central Florida, and around Orange County. Harrison said aerial mosquito spraying is a routine practice during Florida’s mosquito season and should not alarm residents. “Aerial applications are nothing residents need to be concerned about. This is a common daily occurrence within the state of Florida, if not in other states as well. During the mosquito season, on any given night somewhere in the state, there is an aerial application taking place,” Harrison said. Florida has reported 296 locally acquired dengue fever cases in 2026, according to state health department surveillance data. The outbreak is concentrated in Hillsborough County, which accounts for 259 of those cases. The statewide total is among the highest reported by any U.S. state in decades. Mosquito control officials say reducing the population of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which can spread dengue, is key to interrupting transmission. “We’re trying to bring down the population of Aedes aegypti, which is the primary vector for dengue, because we want to interrupt that transmission cycle. And that’s going to give us the best, public health protection to residents,” Harrison said. State health officials have also confirmed a dengue-related death in Hillsborough County. The patient’s identity has not been publicly released. Orange County Mosquito Control is asking county leaders to approve $150,000 to carry out the planned aerial spraying over Orange County

Some words may be mispronounced. Facebook Twitter Bluesky WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter Bluesky WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save For a state whose government officially doesn’t believe climate change is real, Florida remains our nation’s busiest climate-change laboratory. The latest test for the Sunshine State is an outbreak of dengue fever, the largest in the U.S. since the 1940s. The numbers are relatively small: 485 cases as of the latest count from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, largely concentrated in Tampa’s home county. But any case of the disease — sometimes called “break-bone fever” because of how it makes sufferers’ bones feel — was rare in the U.S. not long ago. It’s too soon to attribute this particular episode to climate change because Florida can certainly be hot enough for a dengue outbreak under any circumstances. But a warming planet is making broader swaths of the planet friendlier to disease-carrying mosquitoes, which spread dengue fever. Florida’s experience today will be an example for places at higher latitudes in the near future. The Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes that spread dengue are most dangerous in sustained temperatures of 26 to 31 degrees Celsius (79 to 88 degrees Fahrenheit), according to a study published this week in the journal Science Advances by researchers from Monash University in Australia. These insects also love high humidity and rainfall (though they can also deal with drought because it means people keep more open containers of water). Florida has always been hot and humid. And the U.S. struggled repeatedly with dengue-like outbreaks before World War II.(Dengue wasn't isolated as a disease until 1943, though it certainly existed long before that.) But a global effort to end yellow fever quashed many mosquito-borne illnesses here for generations. Dengue didn’t return to Florida until 2009, when a handful of people caught it in Key West. Since then, the state has been the mainland’s runaway dengue leader, with 606 locally acquired cases and nearly 4,200 travel-associated cases between 2010 and 2025, according to the CDC. Second on the list is California, with nearly 2,600 mostly travel-related cases. None of them approach Puerto Rico, with more than 42,000 cases. But there’s plenty of time to start gaining ground. As my Bloomberg Opinion colleague Lara Williams has documented many times, global heating has expanded the territory of the mosquitoes that carry dengue, malaria, chikungunya, Zika and other diseases. Dengue was endemic to just nine countries 50 years ago. Now it’s in 140. A hotter planet is also boosting the numbers and range of ticks that carry Lyme, encephalitis, anaplasmosis and other horrors. And the hotter the planet gets, the more land these pests can conquer. Even under less-than-extreme greenhouse-gas emissions scenarios, the number of humans at risk of dengue will be 2.3 billion greater in 2080 than in 2015, according to the Monash study. That means 6.1 billion people, roughly the entire global population in 2000, will be regularly exposed to the disease by 2080. But human behavior and climate-change effects also reinforce each other. The steady rush of people into hot places like Florida and Texas helps explain the recent and expected future rise in dengue exposure, the Monash study noted. The (justified) end of widespread DDT spraying gave mosquitoes another tiny toehold. That means people also have the means to fight back, as we learned with yellow fever. Decades of education and billions of dollars of investment in prevention and treatment have helped slow the scourge of malaria, the global incidence rate of which fell by more than a third between 2000 and 2016, while the death rate fell by 60% (though population growth means the number of malaria cases is still rising). Increasing urbanization and economic well-being also help curb that disease. “Houston should be a malaria zone,” Columbia University professor Jeffrey Shaman, a climatologist and infectious-disease specialist who studies mosquito-borne diseases, told me. “It’s swampy, warm, and has lots of opportunities for mosquitoes to do their thing. But they don’t, and the reason is development.” But the Aedes mosquitoes actually thrive in urban environments, Shaman and the Monash study pointed out. Fighting dengue will require different weapons. Alphabet Inc.’s Google, Monash University’s World Mosquito Program and other groups have programs to infect and release mosquitoes with a bacteria called wolbachia, which can curb bug populations, at least temporarily. The Environmental Protection Agency has been sitting for months on a Google request to release infected mosquitoes in California and Florida. But President Donald Trump last week ordered his government to speed up any efforts to rein in all the mosquito- and tick-borne diseases terrorizing boggy Washington, DC, and eventually the rest of the country, which could help. Florida is already running its own experiments. Lee County, home of Fort Myers, has been releasing wolbachia-infected mosquitoes since 2017, the Miami Herald reported. It’s also using radiation to sterilize male bugs and delivering them to unsuspecting mates by plane and drone. The county currently has just 11 dengue cases, though it’s 120 miles south of Tampa. Wolbachia isn’t a perfect solution and isn’t effective everywhere. People also tend to get weirded out by the idea of Frankensquitoes buzzing around, as the Florida Keys discovered when it proposed using genetically modified bugs to curb populations. The best approach, then, is all of the above, as Williams has written. That starts with slowing down mosquito-friendly global heating. And it includes surveillance and warning systems to go along with bacteria, radiation, drones, (safe) pesticides, mosquito-eating fish and whatever else is handy. People need to get in the habit of drying out bird baths and other water containers where mosquitoes breed. Anything that gives humans and mosquitoes fewer chances to interact is worth trying, Shaman said. “That’s the name of the game for controlling outbreaks.” And if it works in Florida, it’s worth trying anywhere. Mark Gongloff is a Bloomberg Opinion editor and columnist covering climate change. He previously worked for Fortune.com, the Huffington Post and the Wall Street Journal.
