records.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Medical Even young, healthy people can go into dengue shock after their fever subsides. Many people with dengue fever mistakenly believe that the absence of fever means they are cured, when in fact this could be the time when dangerous complications begin to appear. Báo Đầu tư•11/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Dengue fever continues to circulate in many localities, posing a risk of severe complications if patients are not monitored and treated promptly. Worryingly, many people are complacent about the initial symptoms, self-treating at home or assuming the disease has subsided after their body temperature returns to normal. According to a report from the Hanoi Center for Disease Control (CDC), from September 25th to the present, the city has recorded 350 cases of dengue fever in 81 wards and communes. Cumulatively from the beginning of the year to the time of this report, Hanoi has had 3,946 cases in 119 wards and communes, with 177 outbreaks recorded, of which 35 are active. Blood concentration - a serious complication of dengue fever. According to Dr. Ngo Van An, Deputy Head of the Internal Medicine Department at MEDLATEC General Hospital, one of the difficulties in detecting and treating dengue fever is that the initial symptoms are easily confused with seasonal flu or other common viral infections. Patients often experience high fever, headache, body aches, and fatigue, leading them to self-medicate without proper examination and testing to determine the cause. Meanwhile, dengue fever becomes particularly dangerous during the period from the 3rd to the 7th day after onset. This is when the patient's fever may subside, but they simultaneously enter a phase of risk for plasma leakage, circulatory disorders, and shock. The case of female patient NVP (24 years old, residing in Hanoi) who was recently admitted to MEDLATEC General Hospital is a typical example. The patient had dengue fever for 6 days, having previously self-tested at home, used a fever-reducing medication containing paracetamol (Efferalgan 500 mg), and drank oral rehydration solution (Oresol). However, just one day after the fever subsided, the patient suddenly felt weak, dizzy, and lightheaded. Noticing the unusual condition, the family quickly took the patient to the hospital for emergency treatment. Upon admission, the patient presented with significant hemodynamic instability, a rapid pulse exceeding 110 beats/minute, and a drop in blood pressure to 80/50 mmHg. Laboratory results showed an elevated hematocrit (HCT) of 43.1%, higher than the laboratory's reference range of 37-42%. HCT is an index reflecting the percentage of red blood cell volume in the blood. In people with dengue fever, this index is elevated, especially when it is higher than the baseline value, which may suggest blood concentration due to plasma leakage. However, the results need to be evaluated in conjunction with clinical manifestations and other indicators to determine the severity of the disease. Upon examination and testing, the doctors diagnosed the patient with severe Dengue hemorrhagic fever, circulatory disturbance, and a risk of hypovolemic shock. The treatment team promptly resuscitated the patient, administered intravenous fluids and electrolytes, used high-molecular-weight fluids as prescribed, and closely monitored hemodynamic and blood gas parameters. After approximately 6 hours of treatment, the patient's blood pressure improved to 120/70 mmHg, heart rate stabilized at 70 beats/minute, and HCT decreased to 39%. Having passed the immediate critical stage, the patient continued to receive inpatient treatment and intensive monitoring. Doctors say this case shows that young people without underlying medical conditions can still experience severe complications from dengue fever. In particular, the absence of fever does not always mean the disease is cured. In critical cases, the Dengue virus can increase vascular permeability, causing plasma to leak out of the blood vessels and reducing circulating volume. If this plasma leakage becomes severe and goes undetected and untreated, the patient is at risk of hypotension, shock, organ damage, and life-threatening conditions. It is noteworthy that these changes can occur while body temperature has already decreased, making it easy for patients and their families to lower their guard. Some cases initially present only with symptoms of fatigue, dizziness, abdominal pain, or vomiting, but circulatory disorders quickly develop afterward. You may also like According to experts, anyone with dengue fever is at risk of developing severe symptoms. However, certain groups require particularly close monitoring due to their potential for complications or difficulties in treatment. For the elderly and those with underlying conditions such as hypertension, cardiovascular disease, or chronic kidney disease, monitoring for dengue fever is often more complicated. Symptoms may be atypical, manifesting as significant fatigue, lethargy, restlessness, confusion, or altered state of consciousness. For patients using anticoagulants or other medications for chronic diseases, doctors need to carefully assess the risk of bleeding, circulatory status, and appropriate treatment options. Patients should not stop or adjust their medication without professional guidance. Young children, especially those under one year old, also need close monitoring because they cannot clearly describe bodily abnormalities. Signs such as unusual crying, refusal to feed, lethargy, cold hands and feet, or decreased urine output should be noted. Overweight or obese children with dengue fever also need careful evaluation. For pregnant women, dengue fever can increase the risk of complications for both mother and fetus, requiring examination and monitoring at an appropriate medical facility. For young, healthy individuals, the biggest risk lies in complacency. The ability to function relatively normally in the initial days or feel better after the fever subsides does not rule out the possibility of the illness progressing to a dangerous stage. Doctors advise that people with dengue fever should be especially vigilant if they experience any of the following signs: extreme fatigue, lethargy, restlessness, or unusual anxiety; severe or persistent abdominal pain, especially in the right lower rib area; frequent vomiting; bleeding gums, nosebleeds, or irregular or heavy menstrual bleeding. More serious symptoms such as vomiting blood, passing black or bloody stools, urinating very little or not urinating for hours, cold extremities, dizziness, or fainting may indicate blood loss, decreased circulating volume, or hemodynamic instability. Patients experiencing any warning signs should seek medical attention immediately, without waiting for the fever to return or for a follow-up appointment. If symptoms such as fainting, difficulty breathing, altered consciousness, significant bleeding, or signs of shock occur, immediate emergency care is required. Besides monitoring the disease progression, proper medication use plays a crucial role in limiting complications. Currently, there is no specific drug routinely used to eliminate the Dengue virus. Treatment mainly focuses on supportive care, appropriate fluid replacement, close monitoring of clinical and laboratory indicators, and early detection of signs of plasma leakage, bleeding, or organ damage. According to MEDLATEC experts, people should not self-medicate with aspirin, ibuprofen, and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) to reduce fever and pain in cases of suspected or confirmed dengue fever, as these drugs can increase the risk of bleeding. Corticosteroids should not be used to treat dengue fever without a doctor's prescription. Paracetamol can be used to reduce fever at appropriate doses, but it is necessary to follow the instructions regarding dosage and intervals between doses to avoid the risk of overdose causing liver damage. Drinking oral rehydration solution (ORS) and supplementing fluids can help replenish lost fluids in patients who are conscious, able to drink, and do not have severe symptoms. However, oral rehydration does not replace assessment and treatment at a hospital if signs of plasma leakage, hypotension, or shock have appeared. Patients should also not self-administer intravenous fluids at home. You may also like Alongside treatment, preventive measures need to be maintained regularly. People should eliminate stagnant water sources, cover household water containers tightly, maintain environmental hygiene, kill mosquito larvae, and take measures to prevent mosquito bites, even during the day. Given the evolving situation with Dengue fever, doctors emphasize that monitoring patients during the fever-reduction phase is particularly important. Early detection of abnormalities in circulation, consciousness, bleeding, and urine output can help patients receive intervention before complications become serious. According to preventive medicine experts, proactive disease prevention is especially important, and vaccination is one of the effective solutions for infectious diseases for which vaccines are available. Regarding dengue fever, according to doctors at the Long Chau Vaccination System, Vietnam uses the Qdenga dengue vaccine. This vaccine is administered to children aged 4 and older and adults, including those who have previously had the disease, and helps prevent all four types of the Dengue virus. The vaccination schedule consists of two doses, administered three months apart. The protective efficacy is over 80%, reducing the risk of hospitalization due to dengue fever by over 90% when the full vaccination regimen is completed. Experts believe the greatest significance of the vaccine lies not only in reducing the risk of contracting the disease but also in limiting severe cases, easing the burden on the healthcare system during outbreaks, and contributing to the protection of high-risk groups such as children. However, the vaccine is not suitable for people who are hypersensitive to any of its components, pregnant women, or breastfeeding mothers. For immunocompromised individuals or those with HIV, please consult a healthcare professional for guidance tailored to your specific situation. records.content: LIVE TV POLITICSTÜRKİYEWAR ON GAZABIZTECHINFOGRAPHICSFEATURESOPINIONWAR ON IRAN HEALTH & EDUCATION 1 min read What is dengue virus? Also known as “breakbone fever,” dengue is a viral disease transmitted to humans through the bites of infected mosquitoes. Share Producer: Hatice Cagla Gunaydin, Graphic Artist: Busra Ozturk / TRT World More than 2.2 million dengue cases and nearly 1,200 deaths were reported across 97 countries and territories in the first eight months of 2026, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). In October, Bangladesh's reported total surpassed 103,000 cases and 300 deaths, while Cuba has recorded 11,235 cases so far in 2026. Florida is also experiencing the largest dengue outbreak in any US state in decades, with nearly 300 locally acquired cases reported this year. About half the world's population is now at risk, with an estimated 100–400 million infections occurring annually, according to WHO. records.content_title: Two new cases of dengue fever found in Florida; aerial spray planned
records.content: News Sports Restaurants Real Estate Opinion Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals STATE Two new cases of dengue fever found in Florida; aerial spray planned The two new confirmed cases are in the Apopka area of Orange County. Michelle Spitzer USA TODAY NETWORK Oct. 13, 2026, 12:14 p.m. ET Florida has reported 298 cases of dengue fever, the largest outbreak in the state in decades. Hillsborough County has the most reported cases, while Orange County is planning aerial spraying to combat mosquitoes. The surge is attributed to warmer temperatures, increased rainfall, and travel from countries with outbreaks. Two new cases of dengue fever, the mosquito-borne illnesses spreading throughout the state, were reported in one Florida county. The Florida Department of Health confirmed the two additional cases in the Apopka area, Orange County officials announced Oct. 12. This brings the statewide total to 298. “We are planning to aerial spray over the next two to three weeks,” Steve Harrison, manager of Orange County Mosquito Control said in a press release. “We will be spraying in the Apopka and Pine Hills areas to kill the Aedes aegypti mosquito, which is the known carrier of Dengue.” Orange County now has a total of five cases. Aerial spraying is expected to reduce the targeted mosquito population by 99%, according to Harrison. “It is very important for residents to ensure that there is no standing water on their property,” Harrison said. “We encourage residents to walk around their yards after a storm and drain any standing water, toss out anything that could hold water, and protect yourself with long sleeves, pants, and EPA-approved mosquito repellent.” What Florida county has the most reported dengue fever cases? Hillsborough County has most of the cases, with 259 reported as of Oct. 3, according to the Florida Department of Health. Other counties with reported cases are Pinellas (20), Miami-Dade (8), Orange (5), Pasco (3), Broward (1) Palm Beach (1) and Polk (1). This year’s 298 cases is the largest outbreak in decades. The previous highest number in Florida was 199 in 2023. Last year, 62 cases were reported in the state. Three Tampa Bay-area counties — Pasco, Hillsborough, and Pinellas — have declared states of emergency to expedite mosquito control operations and cut through paperwork for emergency response. What's causing the Florida outbreak of dengue fever? One reason for the surge in dengue cases is because of a combination of "climatic and human factors that create ideal conditions" for the types of mosquitoes that spread dengue, West Nile and the chikungunya viruses, said Eva Buckner, associate professor and extension specialist with the UF/IFAS Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory via email Sept. 23. Those factors include warmer temperatures, increased rainfall and standing water, and human travel from other countries with outbreaks. Health data show that 215 of the 262 Florida cases acquired from outside the country were people who had recently traveled from Cuba. Most of the cases were DENV-2, one of the disease's four serotypes and the serotype behind Cuba's current epidemic, where fuel shortages are hampering fumigation efforts, according to Forbes. What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. C.A. Bridges and Cheryl McCloud, journalists for the USA TODAY Network-Florida's service journalism Connect team, contributed to this report. Michelle Spitzer is a journalist for The USA TODAY NETWORK-FLORIDA. As the network’s Rapid Response reporter, she covers Florida’s breaking news. records.content: Start Sport Switzerland International Football People MyTech Lifestyle Start Sport Switzerland International Football People MyTech Lifestyle LifestyleFlorida has seen more dengue cases than it has in decades Health Florida has seen more dengue cases than it has in decades The range of mosquitoes that transmit the dengue virus continues to expand. (Featured image) Keystone The state of Florida is currently reporting more cases of dengue fever than it has in decades. An elderly woman died after contracting dengue fever. Keystone-SDA 13.10.2026, 05:32 According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), more than 500 cases have already been reported this year, including about 280 local transmissions. The remaining cases occurred during travel. The majority of cases are reported in the area surrounding the Tampa metropolitan area, where an elderly woman died in September after contracting dengue fever. Several municipalities in the region have declared a state of emergency. Also known as “bone-breaking disease” Dengue fever—sometimes called “breakbone fever” because of the pain it causes—is transmitted by certain species of mosquitoes and is widespread in tropical and subtropical regions. Infection with the virus can cause symptoms such as high fever, nausea, and severe headaches and body aches, but in most cases, the illness resolves without lasting effects. In a small percentage of cases, a severe, potentially life-threatening form of the disease develops. Local dengue outbreaks are not unusual in Florida—but on this scale, they certainly are. The highest number of cases to date was recorded in 2023, when there were just under 200. Because the range of the mosquitoes that transmit these diseases continues to expand, an increasing number of local infections are now being reported even outside the tropics and subtropics. In Europe, according to the EU health agency ECDC, Italy and France have reported such local infections so far this year. To date, no locally transmitted cases of tropical diseases such as dengue, chikungunya, or Zika fever carried by tiger mosquitoes have been recorded in Switzerland, as the Federal Council announced in late September. Article will play after ad... Playing in :00 A A A Kaua‘i mosquito trapping (Aug. 25, 2022). PC: Hawaiʻi Department of Land and Natural Resources The Hawai‘i Department of Health reports identifying a new travel-related dengue virus case on Oʻahu, bringing the total number of dengue cases in the state to eight for 2026. All of the cases have involved travel to Pacific Island countries and territories. The affected individual was exposed to the virus while traveling in a region where dengue is common. No connection to any prior cases in Hawaiʻi have been found. Health department teams have been deployed to conduct inspections and implement mosquito control measures in the affected area. Dengue virus is transmitted from an infected person to a mosquito and then to another person. Due to the circumstances of this case, the expected risk of transmission is low. However, with recent heavy rain, this case is a reminder for the public to eliminate standing water as much as possible. Reducing standing water helps prevent mosquito breeding and can reduce the risk of local transmission of vector-borne diseases. More information about mosquito control is available on the Vector Control Branch website. Dengue is a year-round risk in tropical and subtropical areas of Central and South America, including Brazil and Mexico; Asia, including the Philippines; the Middle East; Africa; and several Pacific islands, including American Samoa, the Federated States of Micronesia, the Republic of the Marshall Islands and the Republic of Palau. Many popular tourist destinations in the Caribbean, including Puerto Rico, are also affected. Some countries are reporting higher-than-usual numbers of dengue cases, including Bangladesh, Bolivia, Cambodia, Costa Rica, Cuba, Ecuador, Kenya, Malaysia, Maldives, Marshall Islands, Panama, Sri Lanka, Vanuatu and Vietnam. Travelers should review current, country-specific travel information for guidance on dengue risk and prevention measures at least four to six weeks before traveling. For current travel health information and guidance, visit the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) travel website. Anyone planning to travel to or who has recently visited an area with dengue risk may be at risk for infection. The CDC advises travelers to take standard precautions when visiting such areas. These include using an Environmental Protection Agency-registered insect repellent, wearing long-sleeved shirts and long pants outdoors, as well as sleeping in air-conditioned rooms, rooms with window screens or under insecticide-treated bed nets. Travelers returning from areas with dengue risk should take precautions to prevent mosquito bites for three weeks. If dengue symptoms develop within two weeks of returning, travelers should seek medical evaluation. Symptoms of dengue can range from mild to severe and include fever, nausea, vomiting, rash and body aches. Symptoms typically last two to seven days. While severe illness can occur, most people recover within a week. Individuals who have recently traveled and are experiencing these symptoms should contact their healthcare provider. Healthcare providers and individuals who suspect dengue infection are advised to call the Disease Reporting Line at 808-586-4586. In areas with suspected or confirmed dengue cases, Health Department vector control personnel conduct inspections and mosquito-reduction activities. Reducing mosquito populations lowers the risk of dengue transmission to others. In areas without reported dengue cases, eliminating mosquito breeding sites around the home is an important preventive measure. Mosquitoes need only small amounts of standing water to breed. Common breeding sites include buckets, water-catching plants such as bromeliads, small containers, planters, rain barrels and even cups left outside. Prevent standing water from collecting around homes and workplaces by emptying containers and other items where mosquitoes can lay eggs. Home News Region Girl, 8, dies of severe dengue in Bacolod News Region Girl, 8, dies of severe dengue in Bacolod By Mae Singuay - Thursday, October 15, 2026 Facebook X Viber Print BACOLOD City — An eight-year-old girl from Barangay Handumanan died of severe dengue, bringing the city’s dengue-related fatalities to six as infections increased by 1.5 percent from last year’s figure, the City Health Office (CHO) reported. The child died on October 3 after suffering complications, including dengue hemorrhagic shock, pulmonary hemorrhage and multiple organ dysfunction syndrome. She was admitted to a hospital on October 1 after experiencing persistent fever, vomiting and abdominal pain, followed by diarrhea. According to the CHO, the girl had previously been hospitalized for dengue at the age of five, making her latest infection her second encounter with the mosquito-borne disease. She developed a high fever on September 28, which temporarily subsided after she was given paracetamol. She initially consulted a private clinic and was diagnosed with a urinary tract infection before her condition worsened. Laboratory results on October 1 showed that her platelet count had dropped to 34,000, indicating a dangerously low level. Despite hospitalization, her condition continued to deteriorate, and she suffered cardiopulmonary arrest on October 3. She was pronounced dead at around 10:30 a.m. Discover more Regional news subscription Western Visayas news Local event coverage The CHO said the fatality was reported to the office on October 4. The latest death brings to six the number of dengue-related fatalities recorded in Bacolod as of Morbidity Week 39, covering September 27 to October 3. The city recorded 891 dengue cases during the period, up 1.5 percent from the 878 cases reported during the same period in 2025. The number of deaths remained unchanged at six. The other fatalities involved a nine-year-old boy and a four-year-old girl from Barangay Mansilingan, an eight-year-old boy from Barangay 16, a five-year-old girl from Barangay Granada, and an eight-year-old girl from Barangay Villamonte. CHO records showed that Barangay Mansilingan had the highest number of dengue cases, with 105, followed by Handumanan with 77 and Estefania with 73. Other barangays with high case counts were Alijis, with 58; Granada, 55; Villamonte and Taculing, 54 each; Singcang-Airport, 53; Tangub, 44; and Banago, 39. Dr. Grace Tan, head of the CHO’s Environmental Sanitation Division, urged residents experiencing fever and flu-like symptoms to seek early medical consultation. She also reminded the public to remain vigilant against dengue and follow the Department of Health’s 4S strategy: search for and destroy mosquito-breeding sites; secure self-protection against mosquito bites; seek early consultation; and support fogging and spraying in areas where these are warranted. Meanwhile, CHO Assistant Department Head Dr. Grace Tan also emphasized the importance of sustained household and community efforts to eliminate mosquito-breeding grounds. Residents were encouraged to practice the city’s “4Ts” of dengue prevention: Taob, Taktak, Tuyo and Takip — turn over water containers, discard accumulated water, keep containers dry, and cover water-storage vessels. The city also urged households to participate in its daily 4 p.m. cleanup habit to remove stagnant water and other potential mosquito-breeding sites. Health authorities advised residents to watch for dengue symptoms, including sudden high fever, severe headache, muscle and joint pain, pain behind the eyes, weakness and skin rashes. Discover more Environment news report Health wellness tips Business news updates Persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, unusual bleeding, dark-colored stools and difficulty breathing are warning signs that require immediate medical attention. The CHO stressed that dengue can progress rapidly and become life-threatening, making early consultation, close monitoring and prompt medical intervention essential to preventing severe complications and deaths./PN RELATED ARTICLESMORE FROM AUTHOR Region Bacolod releases P13.6M MassKara subsidies for participating barangays, schools Region Woman’s body found in sack in Talisay; 2 suspects arrested Region Molo lodging house room boy dies; police rule out foul play LEAVE A REPLY Cancel reply Please enter your comment! healthcare professionals from public hospitals and treatment facilities on dengue case management ISLAMABAD, Oct 09 (APP):The World Health Organization (WHO) has trained doctors and healthcare professionals from public hospitals and treatment facilities on dengue case management The focus of the training is on updated clinical guidance, early detection and timely treatment to prevent severe complications and save lives. The training aimed to strengthen healthcare professionals’ capacity to identify dengue symptoms, monitor warning signs and provide appropriate clinical care in line with updated recommendations and global best practices. Emphasizing the importance of preparedness and early intervention, WHO highlighted that timely diagnosis, close monitoring of patients and prompt management of warning signs were essential to reducing the risk of severe dengue and improving patient outcomes. The initiative underscores the importance of strengthening clinical capacity and ensuring effective management of dengue cases, particularly during periods of increased transmission. The department’s latest W.I.L.D. (water- and food-borne diseases, influenza, leptospirosis, and dengue) diseases report also listed 19 new cases of influenza-like illness (ILI) and four cases of severe acute respiratory infection (SARI). No new cases of cholera, typhoid fever, confirmed COVID-19, or leptospirosis were reported on Oct. 12. LEARN MORE » Sections বাংলা Thursday, October 15, 2026 Today's Paper Video e-Paper Second Edition Contact Sections Home Frontpage Asia City World OP-ED Editorial Business Global Business Commercial Capital Sports Countrywide Featured Sex & Relationship Student Voice LitScape Life Style Reciprocal Teens & Twenties In Vogue Food & Nutrition Bookshelf Entertainment Back Page × Facebook Twitter Pinterest Home Frontpage Published: 01:04 AM, 10 October 2026 Health experts urge early testing, timely treatment to reduce dengue deaths Observing that most dengue deaths are linked to delayed diagnosis and hospitalisation, health experts have called for early testing, timely treatment and greater public awareness of the disease's warning signs to help reduce fatalities from the mosquito-borne illness. They said many dengue patients who die in hospitals arrive at a late stage, leaving doctors with little time to provide effective treatment. "Most of the patients reach us so late that we hardly get time to provide treatment. They arrive in an irreversible condition and, unfortunately, we cannot save them," said Professor Shahnoor Sharmin Munni, head of the Dengue Unit at Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH), BSS reports. Discover more Get Health Tips health Health She said many people still believe dengue testing should be done only after three days of fever, while some become less alert when the fever subsides. "In dengue, a patient may become seriously ill after the fever comes down. Many people remain at home thinking that the danger has passed, but the patient may actually go into shock at that stage," Prof Munni said. She identified three key areas of public awareness: when to undergo dengue testing, what to do when fever subsides and how to recognise warning signs. She added that greater awareness could help narrow the gap between the onset of complications and receiving medical care. Echoing Prof Munni, Mugda Medical College Hospital (MMCH) Deputy Director Dr Muhammad Nurul Islam urged people to seek medical attention as soon as fever develops and get tested if dengue is suspected. He said dengue, a mosquito-borne viral disease, often begins with sudden high fever, body aches, weakness and loss of appetite and warned that a fall in fever after two or three days should not necessarily be considered a sign of recovery. "In dengue, the most dangerous complication is plasma leakage, which can continue even after the fever subsides," Dr Islam said. According to him, plasma leakage causes the fluid component of blood to move out of the blood vessels, reducing circulating blood volume. If the loss becomes significant, a patient can develop shock, characterised by a weak or undetectable pulse, low blood pressure and severe weakness, he said. Discover more Check Symptoms Find Grief Support Death "Without timely intervention, the condition can become fatal," he said. Calling for early diagnosis, Dr Islam said different tests can be useful at different stages of the illness, including the NS1 antigen test in the early phase and antibody tests such as IgM and IgG at later stages. "If dengue can be detected at an early stage, most cases can be managed at home under the national guidelines and do not necessarily require hospital admission," he said. Regarding treatment, the physician said many dengue cases can be managed with adequate rest, nutritious food and sufficient oral fluids, along with paracetamol for fever and body aches. Patients should continue to get adequate rest and drink suitable fluids such as water, lemon drinks, coconut water, fruit juice and soup even after the fever subsides, he said, warning that returning to strenuous physical activities immediately after fever comes down could be risky if plasma leakage is continuing. Dr Islam strongly advised against taking antibiotics or other painkillers without medical advice, saying antibiotics act against bacterial infections, whereas dengue is caused by a virus. "There is no role for antibiotics in treating dengue itself," he said, urging patients to consult registered physicians and follow national treatment guidelines. Dr Islam also cautioned against taking painkillers other than paracetamol, saying drugs such as aspirin and some other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can increase the risk of bleeding, particularly when platelet counts are low. Discover more Find Treatments Seek Counseling Find Hospitals Warning signs of severe dengue include bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in the stool or vomit, abnormal vaginal bleeding and bleeding under the skin, Dr Islam said. On fluid therapy, he stressed that oral and intravenous (IV) fluids should not be treated in the same way, saying IV fluids should only be administered under the supervision of a registered physician. "Both too little and too much fluid can be dangerous," he said, explaining that inadequate fluid replacement can contribute to shock, while excessive IV fluid can cause fluid overload and potentially lead to heart failure. Kurmitola Multicare Specialized Hospital (KMSH) Director Brigadier General Md Saydur Rahman also encouraged early diagnosis, saying not every dengue patient requires hospital admission if the disease is detected at an early stage. Only around 10 to 15 percent of patients with more serious symptoms, including bleeding, severe diarrhoea or vomiting that cannot be controlled, require hospitalisation, he said. Observing that low platelet counts and plasma leakage have traditionally been major concerns in dengue cases, Saydur Rahman said doctors are now seeing more patients with cardiac and liver-related complications. Such complications can sometimes become life-threatening, he said, urging people to seek treatment as soon as possible. Meanwhile, Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) Director (Hospital and Clinics) Dr Md Nurul Islam said adequate quantities of dengue diagnostic kits and intravenous fluids, particularly saline, are currently available at hospitals up to the upazila level across the country. The government is therefore encouraging people to seek testing at local health facilities as soon as possible after developing fever so that dengue can be identified early and appropriate treatment can begin without delay, he said. "There is no fixed rule that a dengue test must be conducted only after three days of fever. We are advising people to get tested as early as possible, depending on the clinical situation," Dr Nurul Islam said. Early treatment can reduce pressure on major hospitals in Dhaka and other large cities, as patients can receive appropriate care at nearby upazila health complexes, district hospitals and medical college hospitals, he added. According to the DGHS, a total of 94,151 people have so far been infected with dengue across the country while 294 died of the disease this year. Doctors report that many of those admitted have critically low platelet counts.For instance, 29-year-old Manisha Rajak, who is 6 to 7 months pregnant, was rushed to Malad’s MW Desai Hospital on Thursday with a high fever, severe muscle and joint pain, and a headache, only to find that there were zero beds available.Hospital officials say all 39 general beds are packed. Dr Pradnya Malgundkar, the medical superintendent, said most beds are occupied by patients with monsoon illnesses, primarily dengue. “Dengue is on the rise, and patients have low platelets. We do not have enough beds to accommodate them,” she said.Even the 10 ICU beds are fully occupied, split between cardiac patients and severe dengue patients. Rajak’s husband, Sunil, told TOI that they had arrived at the hospital around 3 pm and had to rush Manisha to Jogeshwari Trauma Hospital themselves at their own expense.As per protocol, the hospital was supposed to arrange an ambulance for her. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like It's Not Salt: Doctors Now Tie High Blood Pressure to a Drink Most Seniors Have before 8AMThe Living Origins Review Undo Dr Malgundkar said that the hospital has only one BMC ambulance, which was serving another patient at the time. “We need another ambulance and have already requested an additional 108 ambulance,” she added.City-based gynaecologist Dr Nandita Palshetkar, a former president of the Federation of Obstetric and Gynaecological Societies of India (FOGSI), said, “Pregnant women with dengue need to be continuously monitored.” Dr Palshetkar has seen at least two cases like Manisha recently. “In one patient, the platelet count fell to around 30,000. Home News Region Girl, 8, dies of severe dengue in Bacolod News Region Girl, 8, dies of severe dengue in Bacolod By Mae Singuay - Thursday, October 15, 2026 Facebook X Viber Print BACOLOD City — An eight-year-old girl from Barangay Handumanan died of severe dengue, bringing the city’s dengue-related fatalities to six as infections increased by 1.5 percent from last year’s figure, the City Health Office (CHO) reported. The child died on October 3 after suffering complications, including dengue hemorrhagic shock, pulmonary hemorrhage and multiple organ dysfunction syndrome. She was admitted to a hospital on October 1 after experiencing persistent fever, vomiting and abdominal pain, followed by diarrhea. According to the CHO, the girl had previously been hospitalized for dengue at the age of five, making her latest infection her second encounter with the mosquito-borne disease. She developed a high fever on September 28, which temporarily subsided after she was given paracetamol. She initially consulted a private clinic and was diagnosed with a urinary tract infection before her condition worsened. Laboratory results on October 1 showed that her platelet count had dropped to 34,000, indicating a dangerously low level. Despite hospitalization, her condition continued to deteriorate, and she suffered cardiopulmonary arrest on October 3. She was pronounced dead at around 10:30 a.m. The CHO said the fatality was reported to the office on October 4. The latest death brings to six the number of dengue-related fatalities recorded in Bacolod as of Morbidity Week 39, covering September 27 to October 3. The city recorded 891 dengue cases during the period, up 1.5 percent from the 878 cases reported during the same period in 2025. The number of deaths remained unchanged at six. The other fatalities involved a nine-year-old boy and a four-year-old girl from Barangay Mansilingan, an eight-year-old boy from Barangay 16, a five-year-old girl from Barangay Granada, and an eight-year-old girl from Barangay Villamonte. Discover more Regional news subscription Western Visayas news Local event coverage CHO records showed that Barangay Mansilingan had the highest number of dengue cases, with 105, followed by Handumanan with 77 and Estefania with 73. Other barangays with high case counts were Alijis, with 58; Granada, 55; Villamonte and Taculing, 54 each; Singcang-Airport, 53; Tangub, 44; and Banago, 39. Dr. Grace Tan, head of the CHO’s Environmental Sanitation Division, urged residents experiencing fever and flu-like symptoms to seek early medical consultation. She also reminded the public to remain vigilant against dengue and follow the Department of Health’s 4S strategy: search for and destroy mosquito-breeding sites; secure self-protection against mosquito bites; seek early consultation; and support fogging and spraying in areas where these are warranted. Meanwhile, CHO Assistant Department Head Dr. Grace Tan also emphasized the importance of sustained household and community efforts to eliminate mosquito-breeding grounds. Residents were encouraged to practice the city’s “4Ts” of dengue prevention: Taob, Taktak, Tuyo and Takip — turn over water containers, discard accumulated water, keep containers dry, and cover water-storage vessels. The city also urged households to participate in its daily 4 p.m. cleanup habit to remove stagnant water and other potential mosquito-breeding sites. Health authorities advised residents to watch for dengue symptoms, including sudden high fever, severe headache, muscle and joint pain, pain behind the eyes, weakness and skin rashes. Discover more Environment news report Health wellness tips Business news updates Persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, unusual bleeding, dark-colored stools and difficulty breathing are warning signs that require immediate medical attention. The CHO stressed that dengue can progress rapidly and become life-threatening, making early consultation, close monitoring and prompt medical intervention essential to preventing severe complications and deaths./PN RELATED ARTICLESMORE FROM AUTHOR Region Bacolod releases P13.6M MassKara subsidies for participating barangays, schools Region Woman’s body found in sack in Talisay; 2 suspects arrested Region Molo lodging house room boy dies; police rule out foul play LEAVE A REPLY Cancel reply Please enter your comment! Gomez - Correspondent / @carlagomezINQ Inquirer Visayas / 10:17 AM October 14, 2026 Share: Bacolod City has recorded its sixth dengue death of the year on Tuesday after an 8-year-old girl from Barangay Handumanan succumbed to severe complications from the mosquito-borne virus. INQUIRER.net stock images BACOLOD CITY — Bacolod City has recorded its sixth dengue death of the year on Tuesday after an 8-year-old girl from Barangay Handumanan succumbed to severe complications from the mosquito-borne virus. The City Health Office said that the child passed away at a Bacolod hospital due to multiple organ dysfunction syndrome secondary to severe dengue, dengue hemorrhagic shock, pulmonary hemorrhage, and unspecified sepsis. The patient’s illness began on September 28 when she experienced intermittent high-grade fevers. Subscribe Health News Florida Tampa officials go door-to-door to share dengue info in 5 hotspot neighborhoods WUSF | By Emma Brisk Published October 12, 2026 at 5:00 AM EDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Listen • 1:37 Emma Brisk / WUSF Code enforcement officers Josh Trimper, left, and David Daubar, right, translate an informative dengue fever flyer to a Spanish-speaking Forest Lake resident on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. The city canvassed urged residents to dump out any standing water, which is how the Aedes aegypti mosquitoes responsible for the virus breed. Most of the breeding spots are abandoned tires. The Florida Department of Health reports the number of locally acquired dengue fever cases in Hillsborough County continue to rise – with 259 confirmed cases since July, which is 36 higher than the previous week’s numbers. Chelsea Kendrick is the epidemiology program manager with the Hillsborough County Health Department. She said the number of cases are likely higher, since only one in four people exposed to the virus show symptoms. ALSO READ: Hillsborough, Pinellas add to dengue tally as mosquito fight continues “We want residents to really look out for fever, headache, nausea or vomiting, and muscle or joint pain," she said. That’s why inspectors and code enforcement officers from the city of Tampa went door-to-door Friday to spread information in five neighborhoods with higher counts of the virus. Emma Brisk / WUSF David Daubar and other Tampa code enforcement officers spent about five hours Friday, Oct. 9, 2026, canvassing neighborhoods that are hotspots for dengue fever. They warned residents and shared preventative measures they can take. They passed out flyers in Southeast Seminole Heights, North Hyde Park, West Tampa, Forest Hills and Sulphur Springs, urging residents to dump out any standing water, which is how the Aedes aegypti mosquitoes responsible for the virus breed. “By all means, we don't want any more breeding grounds for this dengue virus,” said Jack Ciucio, Tampa’s district supervisor of code enforcement. “It's out there, and it's spreading a lot quicker than we actually thought.” The city threw Mosquito Dunks – floating, doughnut-shaped tablets that kill mosquito larvae – into bodies of water. They can be used in any stagnant water, since they don’t harm other biosystems in the environment. Emma Brisk / WUSF Inspectors dropped these Mosquito Dunks into any large body of water they saw across the five neighborhoods they canvassed Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. These mosquito control pellets are safe for the environment and kill off most larvae. City officials warn that even a bottle cap of standing water that has been sitting out for a week is big enough for mosquitoes to breed. Their recommendations include: Empty or cover anything that could hold water outside your home. This includes buckets, toys, pools, birdbaths, trash or recycling containers, boat or car covers, roof gutters, coolers, pet dishes and tires. Apply insect repellent to any exposed skin and on your clothes. Use air conditioning and keep screens on all windows. If you have a body of water you can’t care for on your own, like an unkempt pool, Ciucio said the city will issue a notice to do so. If you don’t, the city could take you to court and put a lien on your property. “For the most part, whenever we issue notice to a property owner, they'll generally take care of it in a quicker manner,” Ciucio said. But most of the breeding grounds come from tires. “[It’s] kind of at the perfect time of the year, unfortunately, where we have a lot of rainfall,” Kendrick said. “These tires can hold large amounts of water.” ALSO READ: Amid dengue outbreak, mosquito control experts are wary of a wet winter fueled by El Niño Over the past three months, Tampa has removed 23 tons of tires – 17 tons were illegally dumped by tire shops, Ciucio said. He said people dump loads of tires at night, leading city officials to have to get out as quickly as possible the next morning to clean them up and prevent more potential breeding grounds. “There's no way of telling who dumped them unless there's cameras,” Ciucio said. The Department of Health has been monitoring 85 tire shops statewide, but only two in Tampa have received citations. records.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Destination Ho Chi Minh City Ho Chi Minh City, October 9th: Dengue fever season warned; a series of power poles obstructing Chu Van An street to be relocated. Dengue fever is in season; a series of power poles are being relocated on Chu Van An Street; gold prices are experiencing slight fluctuations; ... these are some of the notable news items related to Ho Chi Minh City in newspapers this morning, October 9th. Báo Sài Gòn Giải phóng•09/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Dengue fever is seasonal. According to Dai Doan Ket newspaper, dengue fever is in season in Ho Chi Minh City, with over 35,700 cases reported since the beginning of the year. At pediatric hospitals, many children are admitted in critical condition, even experiencing shock, gastrointestinal bleeding, or respiratory failure. According to the Ho Chi Minh City Center for Disease Control (HCDC), in week 39, the city recorded 1,491 cases of dengue fever, equivalent to the average of the previous four weeks. From the beginning of 2026 to week 39, the total number of cases is 35,714. Some areas with high numbers of cases per 100,000 people include Con Dao Special Zone, Chanh Phu Hoa, and Minh Thanh. The Intensive Care and Toxicology Department of Children's Hospital 1 is treating several severe cases of dengue fever. Experts affirm that dengue fever has different stages of progression. When a child's fever subsides, it's not important to stop monitoring; on the contrary, families need to continue observing the child's condition, especially from the 3rd to the 6th day of the illness. Associate Professor, Doctor Pham Van Quang expressed concern about the fact that many children are brought to the hospital quite late. By the time they are admitted, the children are already in severe shock, and some even have multiple organ damage and failure, making treatment more difficult. According to the Ho Chi Minh City Center for Disease Control (HCDC), in week 39, Ho Chi Minh City also recorded 1,538 cases of hand, foot, and mouth disease, a sharp increase of 63.8% compared to the average of the previous four weeks. The total number of hand, foot, and mouth disease cases accumulated from the beginning of 2026 to week 39 is 36,676. Communes and wards with a high number of hand, foot, and mouth disease cases per 100,000 people include Con Dao Special Zone, Binh Khanh, and Hiep Phuoc. Gold prices today at Mi Hong, SJC, PNJ, and DOJI. As of 8:30 AM this morning, gold prices in Ho Chi Minh City have fluctuated slightly. Today's gold prices in Ho Chi Minh City show a buy-sell spread of 1.5-4 million VND per ounce, depending on the type of gold and the trading unit. Gold price chart for Mi Hong, SJC, PNJ, and DOJI on October 9th. Image created with AI assistance. According to the Lao Dong Newspaper, at Mi Hong Company, SJC gold bars are listed at 141.3 million VND/ounce for buying and 142.8 million VND/ounce for selling. Gold rings are also listed at 141.3-142.8 million VND/ounce (buying - selling). At SJC Company, gold bars are listed at 140.8-143.8 million VND/ounce (buying - selling). Gold rings are listed at 140.8-143.83 million VND/ounce. At PNJ, gold bars are listed at 140.0-143.0 million VND/ounce, while gold rings are priced at 139.5-142.5 million VND/ounce. At DOJI, gold bars are listed at 140.0-143.0 million VND/ounce. Gold rings are priced at 139.0-143.0 million VND/ounce. The buy-sell spread for gold bars at Mi Hong is 1.5 million VND/ounce, while SJC, PNJ, and DOJI all have a spread of 3 million VND/ounce. For gold rings, the spread is 1.5 million VND/ounce at Mi Hong, 3.03 million VND/ounce at SJC, 3 million VND/ounce at PNJ, and 4 million VND/ounce at DOJI. DOJI gold rings have the highest buy-sell spread. People flock to the high-quality Vietnamese goods fair to "hunt" for discounted ceramics, vegetarian products, and more. The festival celebrating 30 years of high-quality Vietnamese products, themed "Pride and Continuation," is currently taking place at Le Van Tam Park, Tan Dinh Ward. You may also like According to Tuoi Tre Online Newspaper, the fair, with 200 booths offering a variety of promotional programs, attracted a large number of customers to experience and shop. Numerous customers choose to buy discounted ceramic products at the Minh Long Ceramics booth - Photo: N.TRÍ Specifically, with promotions applied to all products, including discounts of up to 30%, the booth of Thien Thanh Spice Company was consistently bustling. Similarly, with a discount policy of up to 30% and a fixed price for products such as bowls, cups, plates, glasses, etc., the Minh Long ceramics booth became lively thanks to the large number of customers immediately after the opening. Customers look for discounted vegetarian products at the Au Lac booth - Photo: N.TRÍ Meanwhile, with a 20% discount applied to over 200 products, from packaged to frozen, the vegetarian food stall of Au Lac Vegetarian Food Production and Trading Co., Ltd. also became bustling with customers browsing and inquiring about products. Similarly, numerous other brands such as Duy Anh Foods' vermicelli and noodles, Tan Nhien rice paper, Vinamilk milk, etc., also applied various promotional policies, discounts, buy-one-get-three deals, and more. Customers sample products at the booth of Thien Thanh Spice Company - Photo: N.XUAN The 30th Anniversary Festival of High-Quality Vietnamese Goods took place from October 8th to 11th with many activities, including experiential and shopping activities at the fair with over 200 booths. Businesses are recruiting en masse, and Ho Chi Minh City is organizing job fairs at 12 locations. The demand for recruitment by businesses in Ho Chi Minh City is expected to increase significantly. The city is organizing job fairs in October simultaneously at 12 locations. In the first nine months of the year, the Ho Chi Minh City Employment Service Center organized 163 job fairs. Photo: TUNG NGUYEN Speaking to Dan Tri Online Newspaper, a representative from the Employment Service Center of the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Labor, War Invalids and Social Affairs said that the unit is coordinating with relevant agencies to prepare for the Job Fair and Job Exchange in October 2026. This job exchange will be organized on a large scale, taking place simultaneously at 12 locations across Ho Chi Minh City on the morning of October 13th (from 7:30 AM to 11:30 AM). According to the Ho Chi Minh City Employment Service Center, this job fair aims to support unemployed workers, self-employed individuals, students, and others in accessing labor market information and finding suitable jobs. At the same time, the program also supports businesses in the city in recruiting personnel for production and business operations in the final months of the year. Notably, this job fair utilizes information technology, connecting online interviews between different locations, making it easier for businesses and job seekers in remote areas to connect and conduct interviews without extensive travel. The Ho Chi Minh City Employment Service Center expects the program to connect thousands of job seekers with businesses in need of recruitment. Relocating a series of power poles will make inner-city roads wider and more spacious. After a series of utility poles were removed from the road, the section of Chu Van An Street passing through Binh Thanh Ward, Ho Chi Minh City, has become less congested, creating favorable conditions for the construction unit to complete the road surface and organize traffic. Gia Dinh Power Company is relocating power poles along Chu Van An Street. On the morning of October 9th, a reporter from Tien Phong Newspaper observed that the utility poles that had previously been located in the middle of Chu Van An Street, in the Binh Thanh ward, had been relocated. The road, now free of the poles, is wider and more convenient for traffic. The relocation of the power poles began on October 7th. The old power poles on Chu Van An Street were removed, returning the site to the construction unit. The relocation of power poles on Chu Van An Street began on October 7th. In late February 2025, the People's Committee of the former Binh Thanh District commenced a project to upgrade and expand a road section approximately 600 meters long. The project has a total investment of over 1,067 billion VND, including nearly 982 billion VND for compensation and land clearance. According to the design, the road section will be widened to 23 meters, comprising 4 lanes. A drainage system, lighting, and landscaping will also be constructed simultaneously. Upon completion, the road surface will be approximately four times wider than its current width. Workers are securing sections of overhead power cables. According to the investor, after the relocation of the power poles is completed, the site will be handed over to continue laying the asphalt, installing guardrails and median strips, completing the road centerline, painting road markings, and organizing traffic lanes. The remaining work is expected to be completed around mid-November 2026. After the utility poles were relocated, Chu Van An Street became wider and more spacious. records.content: Dinamani Kannada Prabha Samakalika Malayalam Cinema Express Indulgexpress Edexlive Oct 14, 2026 11:04 PM Subscribe E-PAPER INDIA WORLD STATES CITIES OPINION EXPLAINER BUSINESS SPORTS GOOD NEWS ENTERTAINMENT VIDEOS LIVE BLOG INDIA WORLD STATES CITIES OPINION EXPLAINER BUSINESS SPORTS GOOD NEWS ENTERTAINMENT VIDEOS LIVE BLOG Trending Links Asian Games 2026 TVS group Dakshina Kannada rename healthy food street food Advertisement Gujarat 87 hospitalised in Gujarat after Statue of Unity Parade as Dengue hits security personnel Special teams are also monitoring health and hygiene conditions at the camps, while specialist resident doctors have been deployed at Gandhinagar Civil Hospital to provide prompt treatment to the admitted personnel. The affected personnel belong to the Border Security Force (BSF), Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) and Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP). Representative Image/ Express Illustrations Dilip Singh Kshatriya Updated on: 09 Oct 2026, 12:11 pm 2 min read Copied AHMEDABAD: Dengue and other fever-related illnesses have affected security personnel who arrived in Gujarat for the Statue of Unity parade in Kevadia, with 87 admitted to Gandhinagar Civil Hospital over the past 10 days. Of them, 50 have recovered and been discharged, while 37 remain under treatment. Meanwhile, one jawan died during treatment after complaining of severe chest pain, with a suspected cardiac arrest being investigated as the cause of death. Health Minister Praful Pansheriya visited Gandhinagar Civil Hospital to assess the condition of the admitted personnel and review the medical arrangements. He met the patients, inquired about their health and held discussions with hospital superintendent Dr Mita Parikh and the treating doctors to ensure that adequate care was being provided. According to the minister, the affected personnel belong to the Border Security Force (BSF), Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) and Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP). They had arrived from Odisha, Jharkhand, Delhi, West Bengal and Chhattisgarh to participate in the parade organised at the Statue of Unity in Kevadia. They were shifted to the hospital after developing fever and other health complaints. Pansheriya said the condition of the 37 personnel still undergoing treatment was stable and improving, adding that none of them was in a critical condition. During the review, the minister directed hospital authorities to ensure uninterrupted treatment, adequate hydration and nutritious food for the personnel. He instructed the medical team to arrange fresh fruits, fruit juice, salads and a balanced diet in accordance with doctors' recommendations. He also reviewed the availability of blood and platelet stocks to meet any emergency requirements during dengue treatment. Emphasising the responsibility of the Health Department, Pansheriya said the personnel who safeguard the country's borders must receive the best possible care while recovering from illness. He directed the hospital administration to ensure that no lapses occurred in their treatment. The minister also expressed grief over the death of a security personnel who was undergoing treatment at the hospital. According to the preliminary account, the jawan suddenly complained of severe chest pain. Doctors conducted an electrocardiogram (ECG), shifted him to the intensive care unit and initiated emergency treatment. However, he could not be saved. Pansheriya said preliminary medical observations suggested that the jawan had continued his strenuous daily exercise routine despite suffering from fever and physical discomfort. This has raised the possibility of a cardiac event, although the exact cause of death remains unconfirmed. The minister said the suspected cardiac arrest or heart attack would have to be assessed in light of the medical findings. The final cause of death will be established after the post-mortem report is received. Meanwhile, the Health Department has intensified preventive measures at the accommodation sites where the security personnel are staying. Under the guidance of Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel, departmental teams are carrying out fogging and insecticide spraying twice daily to control mosquito breeding and reduce the risk of further infections. Special teams are also monitoring health and hygiene conditions at the camps, while specialist resident doctors have been deployed at Gandhinagar Civil Hospital to provide prompt treatment to the admitted personnel. With 37 personnel still receiving medical care, the focus remains on their recovery, close monitoring and preventing further infections. The circumstances surrounding the jawan's death are also awaiting confirmation through the post-mortem findings.
